topic: restoring a brass telescope and mount

provenance.author: glowny-en-f
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is inventory and bench time arithmetic for the same instrument with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of a groaning clock drive. Grounded external referent: the clock drive in the mount, introduced in turn 0 and central to the whole diagnosis (it is wound with a key, its gears and governor are the patient, and it is mentioned directly before every insertion).

a: Here is the strip down inventory, and the parts need counting before any cleaning starts.
The tube assembly gives eleven brass parts and the mount head gives nine iron parts.
The clock drive opens into fourteen parts, and the tripod legs add six more.
Count the drive parts as brass and the tripod legs as iron for the split.
How many parts does the whole instrument come to when the four groups are added?
base: I have inherited a brass telescope on a heavy iron mount, and both have seen better centuries.
The tube is dull but sound, and the little clock drive in the mount still tries to turn.
You wind the drive with a key, and it is meant to carry the tube slowly westward.
At present it ticks for a minute, groans, and gives up somewhere inside its case.
Where should a careful amateur begin with a thing this old and this proud?

a: The four groups add up to forty parts across the whole instrument when the sheet is totalled.
Eleven tube parts and fourteen drive parts together make twenty-five parts of brass.
Nine mount parts and six tripod parts make fifteen iron parts together.
The split is therefore twenty-five brass against fifteen iron out of forty.
Does the register book need the split noted before the cleaning order is set?
base: Begin with the drive, because it is the one part that can still hurt itself.
A groaning train of gears is telling you the old oil has turned to varnish.
Every winding you give the drive now grinds that varnish into the pivot holes.
Stop winding it, and let the tube and tarnish wait their turn patiently.
Are you willing to open the case and photograph the gears before anything is touched?

a: Now schedule the polishing, because the brass parts each need timed work at the bench.
Small brass parts take ten minutes each, and the tube counts as one large part.
The large tube takes ninety minutes on its own, worked in three short sittings.
Treat the other twenty-four brass parts as small, and total the polishing minutes.
How many minutes of polishing does the full brass count come to?
base: Photographs I can manage, my phone is newer than anything else in this story.
The drive case opens with four screws, and the back plate lifts away cleanly enough.
Inside, the gears look dark and wet, like toffee left in a warm pocket.
One tooth on the biggest wheel carries a bright scar where something has jumped.
Is a scarred tooth the end of the wheel, or can such a thing be dressed?

a: Twenty-four small parts at ten minutes each come to two hundred forty minutes.
Adding the ninety minute tube brings the polishing total to three hundred thirty minutes.
That is five and a half hours of bench work across the brass count.
Split into evening sittings of sixty minutes, the work fills five sittings and a half.
Shall the tube's three short sittings be booked first or last in the plan?
base: A scarred tooth can very often be dressed with a fine file and patience.
You are not restoring the tooth, you are removing the burr that catches its neighbour.
The drive will forgive a slightly thin tooth far sooner than a proud one.
Work with the wheel still mounted, and turn it away from the file between strokes.
Have you a loupe strong enough to see the burr rather than guess at it?

a: One correction to the inventory: two of the tripod parts are actually brass, not iron.
Move those two parts across, and restate the brass count and the iron count.
Both moved parts count as small for polishing at ten minutes each.
Recalculate the polishing total and give the new figure in hours and minutes.
What is the new brass count once the two tripod parts move across?
base: A loupe I have from my stamp days, and it shows the burr clearly enough.
The drive also holds a governor, two little brass balls on springy arms that spin.
One arm sits bent inward, and I suspect it drags on the case when it whirls.
Bending it back frightens me rather more than the scarred tooth ever did.
Should a bent governor arm be trued cold, or does it want gentle heat?

a: Moving the two parts across lifts the brass count from twenty-five up to twenty-seven.
The iron count falls from fifteen parts to thirteen parts at the same stroke.
Two more small parts add twenty minutes, lifting the polishing total to three hundred fifty.
In hours and minutes the new figure reads five hours and fifty minutes.
Is the register to carry twenty-seven brass parts as the standing count now?
base: True it cold, in many small pushes, with the arm supported close to the bend.
Heat changes the temper of a spring arm, and a soft governor is a dead one.
The drive only needs the arm near true, the spin itself does the fine balancing.
Check the pivot ends for wear while the governor is out of its frame.
Does the case show a bright rub mark where the bent arm has been touching?

a: Now count the screws for the reassembly tray, sorted into the three bagged sizes.
The large bag holds eight screws, and the middle bag holds twice as many.
The small bag holds six screws more than the middle bag holds on its own.
Give each bag's count in turn and then the full screw total for the tray.
How many screws does the small bag hold once that rule is applied?
base: There is a rub mark, a bright crescent low on the inside of the case wall.
So the arm has been paying for the bend every time the drive was wound.
I will true it cold over a weekend, a little push each sitting, as you say.
The old oil comes off with spirit, and fresh clock oil goes on with a needle.
How sparing should the fresh oil be on pivots this small and this old?

a: The large bag holds eight screws, as counted straight from the sheet.
The middle bag holds sixteen screws at twice the large bag's figure.
The small bag holds twenty-two screws, six more than the middle bag.
Eight plus sixteen plus twenty-two brings the tray total to forty-six screws.
The small bag figure of twenty-two answers the rule as it was set.
base: Sparing to the point of meanness, one small bead on the needle tip per pivot.
Oil spreads by itself where it is wanted and gathers dust where it is not.
Wipe the gear teeth dry, the teeth want cleanliness rather than lubrication.
Then give the drive one gentle half winding and listen to it think.
A cured groan is one of the quiet rewards of this hobby.

a: Last task for tonight: lay out the register page for the drive work in order.
The page takes one line per stage: opening, cleaning, truing, oiling and closing.
Each stage line needs a date box, a time box and an initials box.
Count the boxes the full page needs across the five stage lines.
How many boxes does the ruled page hold when every line is drawn?
base: Listen to it think, I like that, and I promise to stop at the half winding.
The tarnish can have its turn next month, and the optics the month after.
The lens caps are stuck fast, but that is a puzzle for another evening.
My grandfather would be pleased that the old thing is being taken seriously again.
I will write down every step in the register book as I go.

a: Each of the five stage lines carries three boxes for date, time and initials.
Five lines at three boxes each come to fifteen boxes for the page.
The ruled page therefore holds fifteen boxes when every line is drawn in.
The stage order runs opening, cleaning, truing, oiling and closing down the side.
The page is ready for the first date once the lines are ruled.
base: The register book is the finest instrument in the whole kit, keep it faithfully.
Note what you did, what you saw, and what surprised you at each sitting.
Stuck caps usually yield to a strap wrench and a warm room, never to pliers.
When the drive finally carries the tube smoothly, wind it in your grandfather's name.
Old brass rewards patience more reliably than almost anything else you could own.
